title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 1.II: Augustine, Jerome’s Critobolus, Julian — help only to be able; Semipelagians likewise withhold the gift of willing itself
pass_a_gloss: Thus Augustine expressed his sentence, De grat. Christi, cap. 5. We ought to know that he believes neither our will nor our action to be helped by Divine aid, but only the possibility of will and of work. And a little after, He does not help that we may will, he does not help that we may act, but only helps that we may be able to will and to act. So that Critobolus who in Jerome sustains the Pelagian’s person, Dialog. advers. Pelag. lib. 3. I do not take away, he says, God’s help, seeing that by his grace we can all that we can, but we bound each within its limits, so that it is God’s grace that he gave power unto free will, and of our will to do or not to do. And this is what Julian said, that the human will receives from itself the existence of a good work. Upon this same rock the Semipelagians also struck: For granting God’s preventing grace, they yet invent such as does not give Willing itself, Believing itself, Persevering itself; but which always commits the event unto free will stirred and helped by God’s grace.
pass_b_english: So Augustine puts his view (De gratia Christi 5): We should know he thinks divine aid helps neither our will nor our act, but only the possibility of willing and working. A little later: He does not help so that we will, nor so that we act—only so that we are able to will and act. Jerome’s Critobolus, speaking as a Pelagian (Dialogi adversus Pelagianos 3), says: I do not remove God’s help, for by his grace we can all we can; but we keep each in its bounds—God’s grace that he gave free will power, and our will to do or not do. That is Julian’s point: the human will takes from itself the existence of a good work. The Semipelagians hit the same rock: granting preventing grace, they still invent a grace that does not give Willing, Believing, Persevering themselves, but always leaves the event to free will stirred and helped by God’s grace.
source_text: Sic ejus sententiam expressit Augustinus, De grat. Christi, cap. 5. Scire debemus, quod nec voluntatem nostram nec actionem Divino adjuvari credit auxilio, sed solum possibilitatem voluntatis atque operis. Et paulo post, Non adjuvat ut velimus, non adjuvat ut agamus, sed tantummodo adjuvat ut velle et agere valeamus. Sic Critobolus ille qui apud Hieronymum sustinet personam Pelagiani, Dialog. advers. Pelag. lib. 3. Non tollo, inquit, Dei auxilium, quippe per cujus gratiam possumus omne quod possumus, sed utrumque suis finibus terminamus, ut et Dei sit gratia quod dedit libero arbitrio potestatem, et nostrae voluntatis facere quid vel non facere. Et hoc est quod Julianus dixit, Voluntatem humanam operis boni existentiam a se accipere. In hunc eundem scopulum impegerunt et Semipelagiani: Nam gratiam Dei praevenientem concedentes, talem tamen fingunt quae non det ipsum Velle, ipsum Credere, ipsum Perseverare; sed quae eventum semper committat libero arbitrio per gratiam Dei excitato et adjuto.
